2003B16.goal: $m$ main courses, $2m$ appetizers, $3$ desserts. We want the least $m$ with at least $365$ distinct dinners ($2003$ isn't a leap year).
2003B16.approach: Need $6m^2\ge365$: $m^2\ge60.9$, so $m=8$ ($6\cdot49=294$ is too few; $6\cdot64=384$ works).
2003B16.bridge: Count dinners as $6m^2$ and compare with $365$.
2003B16.recognize: "Different each night": total combinations at least the number of nights.

2003B17.goal: A sphere of radius $r$ melts to $75\%$ of its volume and exactly fills a cone of radius $r$. We want $h:r$.
2003B17.bridge: Set the melted volume equal to the cone volume.
2003B17.shortcut: Without melting loss it would be $4:1$; $75\%$ gives $3:1$.
2003B17.recognize: Shape-to-shape volume transfers: set the volumes equal.

2003B18.goal: For even $n$, $(n+1)(n+3)(n+5)(n+7)(n+9)$ is a product of $5$ consecutive odd numbers. We want the largest integer dividing it for every even $n$.

tools.name: Guaranteed factors
tools.fact: 5\text{ consecutive odds hit every residue mod }5\text{ and mod }3
tools.why: Odd numbers step by $2$, which is invertible mod $3$ and $5$.

2003B18.approach: $3$ and $5$ always divide it, so $15$ does. To see nothing larger works, compare $n=2$ ($3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\cdot11$) with $n=10$ ($11\cdot13\cdot15\cdot17\cdot19$) and $n=12$ ($13\cdot15\cdot17\cdot19\cdot21$): the only factor common to all three is $15$.

steps.title: Always divisible by 15
steps.explain: Among $5$ consecutive odd numbers, one is a multiple of $5$ and at least one a multiple of $3$.

check.q: Why does one of five consecutive odd numbers divide by $5$?
check.why: Steps of $2$ cycle through all residues mod $5$.

steps.title: Nothing more
steps.explain: $n=10$: $11\cdot13\cdot15\cdot17\cdot19$ has exactly one $3$ and one $5$, so $9$, $25$ and $7$ are out. $n=12$ has no factor $11$. So $15$ is the most that always divides.

2003B18.bridge: Show $15$ always works; use a couple of cases to rule out more.
solution: Five consecutive odds include a multiple of $3$ and of $5$.
2003B18.shortcut: Test two cases and take the gcd: $\gcd(3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\cdot11,\ 11\cdot13\cdot15\cdot17\cdot19)=165$; a third case $n=12$ removes the $11$, leaving $15$.
traps: Answering $165$ from only two test cases.
2003B18.recognize: "Largest integer always dividing": guaranteed residues, then counterexamples.

2003B19.goal: Big semicircle radius $2$ on $AB$; three unit semicircles centred at $-1,0,1$ along $AB$. We want the big semicircle minus the union of the small ones. Overlaps are half-lenses.

tools.name: Half-lens
tools.why: Two unit circles with centres $1$ apart overlap in a lens of $\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$; half is above $AB$.

tools.name: Union by inclusion–exclusion
tools.why: The outer semicircles don't overlap each other.

check.q: What is the lens area of two unit circles with centres $1$ apart?

2003B19.bridge: Union of the small semicircles via half-lenses.
2003B19.shortcut: Check magnitude: $\approx2.80$, a bit under half of $2\pi$.
traps: Using full lenses instead of halves.
2003B19.recognize: Overlapping semicircles on a line: inclusion–exclusion with half-lenses.

2003B20.goal: Rectangle $AB=5$, $BC=3$; $F,G$ on $CD$ with $DF=1$, $GC=2$ (so $FG=2$). Lines $AF$ and $BG$ meet at $E$ beyond $CD$. We want $[AEB]$. Triangles $EFG$ and $EAB$ are similar.

tools.name: Similar triangles
tools.why: $FG\parallel AB$; $h$ is the height of $E$ above $AB$.

2003B20.recognize: Lines from a base through a parallel segment: similar triangles with a shared apex.

2003B21.goal: A bag has $2$ red, $2$ green. Each step: draw a bead, replace it with red. We want $P(\text{all red after }3\text{ steps})$. Both greens must be drawn.

tools.name: Paths
tools.why: The two greens must be drawn in two of the three steps.

check.q: After one green is replaced, what is $P(\text{green})$ next?

2003B21.shortcut: Probabilities change after each green draw — always update the state.
2003B21.recognize: Changing-urn problems: track the state and list paths.

2003B22.goal: A clock chimes $1$ at each half hour and $h$ at $h$ o'clock. Starting 11:15 AM Feb 26, 2003, we want the date of the $2003$rd chime. Count to midnight, then by whole days.

tools.name: Chimes per day
tools.why: Two cycles of hours plus $24$ half-hours.

2003B22.approach: Through midnight ending Feb 26: $1+12+12+66+12=103$ chimes. $2003-103=1900=10\cdot180+100$. Ten full days (Feb 27–Mar 8), then the $100$th chime of Mar 9.

steps.title: Days
steps.explain: $1900=10\cdot180+100$. After Feb 27, 28, Mar 1–8 ($10$ days) we need $100$ more, which happens during Mar 9 ($100<180$).

check.q: Which date is $10$ days of chimes after Feb 26 ends?

2003B22.bridge: Count to midnight, divide the rest by $180$.
solution: $103$ chimes through the end of Feb 26.
$10$ full days end with Mar 8; the $2003$rd chime is on Mar 9.
2003B22.recognize: Periodic counting: count to a clean boundary, then use the period.

2003B23.goal: Regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ of area $1$. We want the area of rectangle $ABEF$. Compare with side $s$.

tools.name: Octagon area
tools.why: Square of side $s(1+\sqrt2)$ minus four corners of $\tfrac{s^2}{4}$.

2003B23.approach: Rectangle $ABEF$: sides $s$ and $s(1+\sqrt2)$, area $s^2(1+\sqrt2)$ — exactly half the octagon.

check.q: What is the distance between opposite sides of a regular octagon of side $s$?
What is the octagon's area in terms of $s$?

2003B23.shortcut: The two trapezoids $BCDE$ and $FGHA$ together equal the rectangle.
traps: Using the area of a square.
2003B23.recognize: Regular octagon sub-regions: express everything in the side length.

2003B24.goal: $x+y,\ x-y,\ xy,\ \tfrac xy$ are in arithmetic progression. We want the fifth term. The common difference is $(x-y)-(x+y)=-2y$.
2003B24.approach: First gives $x=\tfrac{3y}{1-y}$; second gives $x=\tfrac{-2y^2}{1-y^2}$. Equating: $3(1+y)=-2y$, so $y=-\tfrac35$, $x=-\tfrac98$. Fifth term $=\tfrac xy+d$.
2003B24.shortcut: Check the terms in fortieths: they rise by $48$ each time.
2003B24.recognize: Mixed-expression APs: equal consecutive differences give a system.
